turns.doctor_question: Besides the memory issues, have you noticed any other changes—like feeling confused about where you are or what time it is, having trouble finding words, or feeling unusually anxious or worried most days?
turns.patient_response:
Well, let me think about that. Confused about where I am? Oh, gosh, no, definitely nothing like that. I mean, I've worked at the same apartment complex for six years now. I know every single inch of that place. I know every boiler room, every crawlspace, every shortcut through the courtyard. Honestly, if you blindfolded me and dropped me in the middle of Building C, I could probably tell you exactly where I was just by the smell of Mrs. Gable's cabbage soup—she makes it every Tuesday, bless her heart, and it just permeates the whole floor. So no, I always know exactly where I am. 

And as for what time it is, well, my dog Buster is basically a furry alarm clock. He has this internal radar that goes off at exactly 5:00 AM for his morning walk and 5:30 PM for his dinner, and he will literally sit there and whine at me if I'm even two minutes late. Plus, in my line of work, you're always looking at the clock, trying to figure out if you have enough time to snake a drain before your lunch break or if you should just wait until after. So time is never really a mystery to me.

Trouble finding words? No, I don't think so. My sister would probably tell you I have the exact opposite problem! I can talk your ear off once I get going, especially if it's a story about one of my crazy tenants. I never forget the names of my tools, either. A basin wrench is a basin wrench, a Phillips head is a Phillips head. I never find myself standing there holding a wrench and not knowing what to call it. The words are all there just fine. 

And as for feeling unusually anxious or worried... I mean, I'm stressed right now, sure. But I think anyone would be, right? Dave pulling me into the office and telling me I might lose this promotion to Senior Tech—that really put the fear of God in me, because I need that pay bump. My truck needs a new transmission, and that's not cheap. So yes, I'm worried about my job, and I get a knot in my stomach when I realize I forgot another work order. But it's not like I'm just sitting around my house biting my nails over nothing, you know? It's a very specific, logical stress about the fact that I keep dropping the ball at work. If I could just figure out how to keep those digital work orders in my head and actually show up when I promise I will, I'd be right as rain. So it really is just the forgetting. That's the only thing that's really out of whack.

It was physical, you know? I could feel it in my pocket. But 11 months ago, these new corporate folks came in and decided we needed to be "modernized." They took away our paper tickets and gave us all these tablets—they're in these thick, heavy black rubber cases so we don't shatter the screens if we drop them on the concrete—and they instituted all this incredibly strict documentation.

Oh, the actual work? No, no, not at all. I remember how to do all of that just fine. It's really like muscle memory at this point, you know? I mean, take a leaky faucet, for example, since you mentioned it. Most of the units in our complex still have these older single-handle faucets—the ones with the little ball assembly inside? I must have rebuilt a thousand of those over the last six years. I don't even have to think about the steps anymore. I know exactly what to do. 

First, obviously, I get under the sink and shut off the hot and cold supply lines—which, let me tell you, half the time those shut-off valves are completely stuck because nobody ever turns them, so I always have to bring my channel locks just to get them to budge. But once the water is off, I just take my Allen wrench, pop off the handle, unscrew the dome cap—sometimes you need a pair of pliers for that if there's hard water buildup, which we have a lot of in this city, it just ruins the fixtures—and then I just pull out the cam and the little rubber seats and springs. Swap in the new ones, put it all back together, and turn the water back on. 

I can do the whole thing in under ten minutes, easy. My hands just know exactly where to go and what tool to grab from my belt next. Same thing with bleeding a radiator or swapping out a garbage disposal or replacing a wax ring on a toilet. The steps are all right there in my head, perfectly clear. I never, ever stand there staring at a pipe wondering what to do next. The physical work is honestly the easiest part of my day! 

Like I was saying before, the problem isn't the doing. The doing is fine. It's just... it's the remembering to actually go to the apartment to do it in the first place. Or remembering to type all those little steps I just told you into that heavy black tablet before I walk out the door. If Dave just pointed at a broken sink and said 'fix it,' I'd have it done perfectly every single time. So, no, I definitely don't forget how to do the repairs themselves. My brain is perfectly fine when my hands are working.
